newsitem.title: USA: LME and Nymex spar over volumes and policy.
newsitem.headline: LME and Nymex spar over volumes and policy.

text.p: Top officials from the London Metal Exchange (LME) and the New York Mercantile Exchange (NYMEX) - the world's leading metal markets, sparred over their respective turnovers and trading policy at an industry gathering here.
At the American Metal Market forum - one of the events surrounding the U.S. copper club week - Nymex Executive Vice-President Neil Wolkoff said the LME's volumes were inflated.
Meanwhile, in response LME Chief Executive David King said that Nymex's plan to open warehouses for delivering copper in Chile, the world's largest producer, would affect the physical market.
But it was the argument over turnovers and market share that underlined the differences in the way that the LME, which has the bigger copper contract, and Nymex trade.
Wolkoff said that LME volume is in reality 37.5 percent the amount portrayed.
"...a huge trick has been played on the market-place," he said.

According to data, the LME's ratio of volume to world production is 40:1, which even after being adjusted by removing position transfers and non-transcational volume that no other exchange includes in its figures, is still 15:1.

Wolkoff said that this exceeds the accepted and normal ratio. There are exceptions, such as gold and silver, but these are often held for investment in huge strategic stockpiles, unlike copper, which is generally produced to be consumed.

However, another exception was aluminium on the LME, which Wolkoff said suffers from the same volume inflation as copper. The adjusted ratio of 15:1 is seven times Nymex's ratio of copper volume to production, he noted.
King said that the LME turnovers do include carry transactions and crosses, but the Exchange is different in other ways.
LME dealers, as well as executing customer orders, trade their own books and take positions. In many cases, therefore, business is "netted out' before it reaches the market.
"This is like comparing apples and pears, or in this case LME swans and Nymex lame ducks," King said.
"If I could give some advice to Nymex I would say it is not size that counts, it is the way that you use it," he added.

Disagreements between Nymex and the LME have been highlighted this last year by the Sumitomo Corp copper trading scandal of the $2.6 billion of unauthorised losses allegedly run up by the Japanese company's head copper trader Yasuo Hamanaka.
However, the two markets and cultures are not entirely at loggerheads, with the LME taking steps to increase data transparancy, and also share information.

"In the past few weeks the LME has passed data on the U.K. regulators, who have passed it on the the U.S. Commodity Trading Futures Commission (CFTC). They can they decide what to pass on to Nymex," King said.
"We think that the two contracts can live side-by-side,' King said referring to the rival copper markets.
